title: Tullo and the Talking Bells
markdown:
In the high craggy mountains, where gardens clung to steep slopes and lakes sparkled like blue jewels, lived an ogre named Tullo. He was as big as a small cottage, skin the colour of rich damp earth, eyes like polished amber. For all his size he was as gentle as a dewdrop and as patient as a peak. His always-with-him friend was Maple, a ram with fleece like spun moonlight and a surprising twinkle in his eyes.

Their home nestled in a valley carved by old glaciers. Life hummed: sheep, clear streams, and the distant chime of the valley’s many bells. The bells chimed for all sorts of reasons — sun over the highest ridge, a cloud shaped like a grumpy badger, or simply because it was Tuesday. Most folk found it normal, if a bit busy. Tullo found the constant ringing rather much. Especially one crisp morning, as the sun began to warm the jagged peaks. Ding-dong-dee, all at once, a jangling chaos from every cliff. Then again, more urgent: dong-ding-da. Enough to make a giant sigh, a rumble through his sturdy stone cottage.

“Honestly, Maple,” Tullo rumbled, pebbles in a brook, bushy eyebrows furrowing, “can’t a fellow enjoy his acorn porridge in peace?” The steaming bowl was quickly forgotten.

Maple, usually content to chew a stray mountain herb, let out a soft questioning bleat and nudged Tullo’s hand. The sound was not just loud. It felt wrong: a frantic edge, a clash that set keen senses on alert.

Soon the whole valley was in a tizzy. Mrs Crumb the baker ran out, flour on her cheeks. “The bells are mad. The mountain’s angry. A terrible storm.”

Old Man Thistlewick, usually asleep by noon, hobbled out on a gnarled stick. “A terrible noisy sign. We must appease the mountain gods.”

Everyone shouted. Some suggested a feast of roasted yams and honey cakes. Others a brave climb to silence the bells with heavy cloaks. Dramatic, loud, and, to Tullo’s mind, missing the point. He observed the rush to judgment, the assumption of anger.

Instead of joining the clamour he scratched his bumpy chin. “Perhaps the bells aren’t angry. Perhaps they’re trying to tell us something. Not shouting. Whispering a message.”

Maple bleated as if to say exactly.

“Let’s go see for ourselves. A quiet investigation might be more useful than a loud argument with the wind.”

Maple trotted beside him, hooves a soft rhythmic clatter. They clambered up paths so steep they seemed to climb into the sky. Wind whispered through ancient firs. Sunlight dappled mossy rocks gold and green. Maple guided them past loose stones and over tricky ledges. “Good boy, Maple.” A large warm hand on a sturdy back. Maple would pause, ears swiveling, then nudge a better route.

Their journey led to the Eaves of Wisdom: a library carved into sheer cliff, hushed reverence, knowledge sleeping in ancient scrolls. Elara Meadowlight greeted them from behind a towering stack, eyes like starlight captured in deepest night, a mind older than the mountains. Her voice was the rustle of parchment.

“Ah, Tullo, and your trusty Maple. I’ve heard the enthusiastic ringing from below. Quite disruptive to quiet contemplation.” Kind smile, a hint of concern.

Tullo explained. “They ring and ring, and no one knows why. The valley folk are panicking, ready to fight or flee. Maple and I think they’re more than noisy. They feel troubled.”

Elara unfurled a brittle parchment, edges crumbling. “The Bell Chimes of Oakhaven. Forged in a time when the mountain’s very breath could be heard. They ring in response to its whispers — subtle shifts, tremors, hidden springs. Silent for centuries, while the mountain slept. This is most unusual.” Starlit eyes met amber. “The bells are ringing because the mountain is restless.”

Restless. Not angry. Not malicious. Unsettled. That made sense. But what was unsettling the great mountain?

As they left, a low rumble shook the ground: not a violent jolt, a deep persistent tremor. More bells, frantic, discordant. Small stones tumbled, bouncing harmlessly off Tullo’s shoulders. The valley below seemed to hold its breath.

Maple’s ears twitched toward a distant higher peak. An urgent bleat. He pointed with his whole body toward the old crumbling tower where the bells hung, a lonely sentinel.

They had to get closer. Around a bend a roar split the air: not thunder, rock and earth giving way. A cascade of rocks, some as big as Tullo’s head, blocked the path to the tower. Dust, broken pine, pulverized stone. The mountain had slammed its door.

Tullo slumped against a moss-covered boulder. “We can’t even get there. The path is blocked. Elara’s words, the valley folk’s fears — nothing seems to fit.” The bells continued their frantic peal from their unseen perch.

Maple was not one to give up. He nudged, then walked to a patch of damp earth at the base of the new rockslide. He sniffed, pawed. Tullo followed. The ground was much wetter than it should be. A tiny trickle, impossibly clear and cold, seeped between newly dislodged rocks.

The mountain’s whispers. The restless earth. An overflowing spring. The bells were not the cause; they were an alarm. Snowmelt from the highest peaks was pushing to the surface, shifting ground beneath the old tower. The tower was wobbling. Foundations disturbed by unseen water.

“Maple, you clever boy. It’s not an attack. It’s not an omen. It’s a plumbing problem. A rather grand one, but a plumbing problem nonetheless.”

He examined the slide, then the seep. He would not smash. He would redirect. With immense strength and the delicate touch of a gardener, Tullo began to shift boulders. He did not clear the path; that was impossible. He created a new safe channel, a gentle course away from unstable ground, a small winding stream toward a lower lush meadow where wildflowers could drink. Maple stood watch, ears swiveling, and once nudged Tullo away from a stone that would have tumbled the wrong way. Water followed the new bed as if it had been waiting for permission. The smell of wet earth and crushed pine rose. Tullo’s porridge-cold hands, used to stillness, found they were good at this too: not fighting the mountain, only offering it another way down.

The last stone settled. The new stream took the overflow. The frantic chiming slowed. Ding. Dong. A long waiting pause. Then deep silence. The bells fell quiet as if they had delivered their message and could rest.

Tullo and Maple stood breathing the newfound peace: wind in firs, the happy gurgle of diverted water.

Below, doors creaked. People peered out, relief and wonder. The silence was more beautiful than any chime.

Against the clear sky a soft white mist swirled around the now-quiet tower, like a gentle hug from the mountain. Tullo smiled, amber eyes crinkling, and looked down at Maple. They did not need to name the lesson. The porridge would still be cold when they got home. The bells would, perhaps, chime again on Tuesday. For now the stream ran where it was meant to, and a ram’s nose had been the wisest book in the Eaves.
characters: Tullo (an ogre), Maple (a ram), Elara (an elf librarian)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
